title: Induction
hook: A clean run of yesterday can make tomorrow look safer than it is.
coreIdea: Induction turns observed cases into a general rule, but the rule can become dangerous when the sample is thin or the break point is hidden.
counterintuition: Experience is useful, but an unbroken run is not a guarantee. A good rule asks how much evidence supports the pattern and what could end it.
tryThisNow: Pick one claim based on repeated experience. Write the sample size, the missing cases, and the condition that would break the pattern.
keyTakeaway: Respect the pattern, then search for its breaking point.

breakdown.fastRead:
The sensor graph sits beside the pension app default-rate test after twelve weeks of steady sign-ups. Nell hears the product team say the default always works. Twelve weeks is evidence. It is not a law.

Induction is the move from observed cases to a general rule. It is how you learn from experience. It becomes an error when a few clean observations are treated as proof that the pattern must continue.

An unbroken run can still be fragile.

The correction is to ask what the run actually covers, what it leaves out, and what condition would break it.
breakdown.deepRead:
The sensor graph in Nell's pension app report climbs in a smooth line. Every weekly release with the new default has lifted enrollment. The team wants to lock the default into the annual plan and stop testing. Nell marks induction risk on the graph because the pattern is strong enough to respect and too narrow to worship.

Induction is not foolish by itself. You cannot make decisions without generalizing from past data. If ten campaigns fail, if five machines break after the same repair, if a route is late every Friday, experience is telling you something. The danger is forgetting the boundary of the evidence. The pattern may hold only for one season, one group, one market, one machine age, or one set of incentives.

A run teaches best when its edge is visible.

Gavin sees the same problem in an ambulance night-shift review. A water sample sits beside a staffing report after eight quiet nights in a row. A manager wants to cut one paramedic because the run has been calm. Gavin marks unbroken-run risk on the sample and asks whether holidays, weather, flu cases, and nearby hospital closures were part of those eight nights.

The question is not whether the past matters. It does. The question is how far the past is allowed to travel. Thin experience can support a test, a warning, or a working rule. It should not become a permanent rule until you know what cases it has not yet faced.

Ask where the pattern has not been tested.
breakdown.fullRead:
The renovation model card is clipped to a brick sample while Leonie studies the budget table. Four similar apartment renovations finished under estimate, and the client wants to approve the fifth with the same contingency. The case looks familiar: same building age, same contractor, same layout. Familiarity starts to behave like certainty.

Induction is one of the mind's most useful shortcuts. You see repeated cases and infer a rule. The door opened the last hundred times the handle turned. The supplier delivered on time for six months. The default setting raised enrollment for twelve weeks. Without this move, every morning would require proof from scratch.

The problem is that a pattern can be clean right up to the moment it breaks. Nassim Taleb's Thanksgiving turkey makes the point brutally: each day of feeding confirms the turkey's belief that humans are friendly, until the day the pattern reverses. The older versions of the example run through Russell and Hume, but the pressure is the same. Past regularity can hide the condition that will end it.

What has this pattern not yet had to survive?

Leonie writes that question on the model card. The four under-budget renovations go in one column. The fifth project's differences go in another: a hidden wall, a new permit rule, a tenant still on site, and winter delivery dates. The past data still matter. They set a starting expectation. But the break points decide whether the old rule can travel. She keeps the old pattern as the baseline and raises the contingency only where the new conditions deserve it.

You can feel the same pressure in a watch retailer waitlist. You are holding a queue ticket while Nolan shows twelve months of waitlist customers accepting the first offered model. Now a price increase is coming, and he wants to assume the run will continue. Nolan must decide whether the black-swan risk is present: the customers may have behaved consistently only under the old price and resale market.

A pattern is not wrong because it can break. It is wrong only when you forget that it can.

The practical move is to turn every induction into three questions. How many cases support this rule? Which cases are missing? What new condition would make the old pattern stop? Those questions do not destroy experience. They give experience a boundary, and a bounded rule is far safer than a confident slogan.

Respect the pattern, then search for its breaking point.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Induction helps people learn from experience, but it can turn too little past data into a false law. Readers need to test the boundary and break point before relying on a pattern.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to use past patterns without turning them into false guarantees.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a run looks clean, then I will list untested users and conditions before making it permanent.
If quiet periods support a staffing cut, then I will check whether hard conditions were present in the sample.
If past data points to a rule, then I will name the break point before acting.
If I say this always happens, then I will ask what cases I have not seen.
